reference.source: Williams Textbook of Endocrinology / endocrine reference literature
clinicalPearls: Causes spontaneous, often postprandial or late-fasting, hypoglycaemia due to autoantibodies against endogenous insulin, in patients who have never received exogenous insulin
A leading cause of autoimmune hypoglycaemia, most frequently reported in East Asian populations
Strongly linked to particular HLA-DR4 alleles and frequently triggered by sulfhydryl (thiol)-containing drugs such as methimazole and alpha-lipoic acid
The biochemical hallmark is markedly elevated total insulin with very high insulin autoantibody titres and a raised C-peptide
Hypoglycaemia occurs when antibody-bound insulin dissociates unpredictably, releasing free insulin at inappropriate times
Often associated with other autoimmune conditions, particularly Graves disease, so a careful drug and autoimmune history is essential
The condition is usually self-limiting: withdrawing the offending drug, dietary measures and, in resistant cases, immunosuppression control symptoms
reference.pathophysiology: In insulin autoimmune syndrome, autoantibodies form against endogenous insulin, typically in genetically predisposed individuals carrying specific HLA-DR4 alleles, and are frequently precipitated by sulfhydryl-group-containing drugs that expose immunogenic insulin epitopes. After a meal, insulin is secreted and largely bound by the circulating antibodies, so glucose initially rises; subsequently the antibody-insulin complexes dissociate in an uncoordinated way, liberating large amounts of free insulin during fasting or the late postprandial period and producing hyperinsulinaemic hypoglycaemia. The high antibody load explains the strikingly elevated measured insulin levels.
additionalDifferentials: Factitious hypoglycaemia from exogenous insulin or secretagogues
Insulin receptor autoantibody (type B insulin resistance) syndrome
additionalInvestigations: Simultaneous glucose, insulin, C-peptide and proinsulin during a hypoglycaemic episode
Sulfonylurea and meglitinide screen to exclude secretagogue ingestion
HLA typing where diagnostic uncertainty persists
Screening for associated autoimmune disease, especially thyroid disorders
Imaging to exclude insulinoma when the antibody result is not confirmatory
redFlags: Severe neuroglycopenia with seizures or loss of consciousness
Recurrent hypoglycaemia refractory to dietary measures
Diagnostic confusion with insulinoma leading toward unnecessary pancreatic surgery
Coexisting decompensated autoimmune disease such as thyrotoxicosis
reference.prognosis: The syndrome is frequently self-limiting and remits within months once the precipitating drug is stopped, although some patients need immunomodulatory treatment for persistent disease.
pitfalls: Misdiagnosing the very high insulin level as insulinoma and proceeding to pancreatic surgery
Overlooking a recently started sulfhydryl-containing drug as the trigger
Failing to measure insulin autoantibodies in unexplained hyperinsulinaemic hypoglycaemia
Attributing symptoms to factitious insulin use without confirmatory testing
references: Endocrine reference literature on autoimmune hypoglycaemia
management: Stop the triggering thiol-containing drug (such as methimazole or alpha-lipoic acid), which alone resolves many cases
Manage hypoglycaemia with frequent small low-carbohydrate meals and alpha-glucosidase inhibitors to reduce postprandial peaks
Reserve corticosteroids or immunomodulatory therapy for persistent or severe disease
Screen for and treat associated autoimmune disorders, especially thyroid disease
Distinguish from insulinoma and from exogenous insulin or secretagogue use before escalating treatment
Monitor for spontaneous remission, which is usual within months, under endocrinology supervision
